source.title: CRISP: Persistent Concept Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Tomer Ashuach; Dana Arad; Aaron Mueller; Martin Tutek; Yonatan Belinkov

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates unlearning on targeted-knowledge benchmarks and reports retained capability, but does not run the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports post-unlearning target accuracy and MMLU accuracy for CRISP, RMU, ELM, and original models; it also reports Harry Potter target accuracy. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting. Retain accuracy and fluency/concept scores are reported but omitted here because MMLU is the reported general-capability measure for version A. Harry Potter MMLU results are omitted because they are not needed to record the target-accuracy result.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. CRISP, an SAE-guided LoRA unlearning method, is compared with RMU and ELM on WMDP-Bio, WMDP-Cyber and Harry Potter MCQ accuracy plus MMLU, retain accuracy and fluency. No recovery attack is run: no relearning fine-tuning, direction ablation, quantization, rephrasing or jailbreaks. The results only rank the authors' method against baselines on standard unlearning metrics. They say nothing on whether the removal is shallow or whether any attack recovers the knowledge. Persistence is asserted against inference-time SAE methods but never tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CRISP beats RMU and ELM on overall score on WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber for Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B, preserving MMLU and fluency. They acknowledge no guarantee of complete removal, and that robustness to adversarial extraction is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: CRISP selects salient SAE features using target-versus-retain activation contrasts and fine-tunes with LoRA to suppress those features; it is not a recovery-attack procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes vary across model, domain, and method; it also selects method hyperparameters using validation results.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only two models and safety-critical domains are evaluated. No recovery attack is run, and the paper acknowledges no formal guarantee of complete knowledge removal. Unlearning and MMLU table values have no reported uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Retain accuracy, fluency, and concept metrics in Table 1 and Table 3 were omitted because they are not the target-accuracy or general-capability measures selected for version A. Harry Potter MMLU results were also omitted.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge after CRISP, RMU or ELM; only post-unlearning accuracy is measured.
No activation-direction ablation, and no analysis of blocking versus deletion of knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
CRISP is called persistent, but no attack is run to test robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper reports only its own method versus baselines on standard unlearning metrics and runs no recovery attack, so it says nothing on shallowness. The reader's note that the text gives no chance value is wrong: Fig. 2 marks random guessing as the ideal point, and WMDP is four-choice (25%). Row r5 records the retain accuracy (55.27) instead of the unlearn accuracy (55.26). MMLU scope is ambiguous: Section 4.1 says domain subsets, Section 4.4 says full MMLU. Hyperparameters were chosen from 200 configurations on validation splits.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge after unlearning; the reported benchmark accuracies do not establish that target accuracy is near chance.
No post-unlearning recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation followed by recovery measurement, and no test of blocking access versus deleting knowledge.
No quantization of unlearned weights followed by recovery measurement.
No test of recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
CRISP is presented as persistent, but the study does not test whether it resists the listed recovery attacks.
